description: Golden-answer eval set for grading quality. Each case is a real bank question plus an answer of known quality and the score range the grader must land in. Run via a parametrized pytest marked 'eval' against the real LLM (costs tokens - run pre-demo / on schedule, not per-commit). Score scale is 0-5. 'expected_flagged' asserts the flagged field when present. Stability rule (tested in code, not per-case): grading the same case twice must land within +/-1.

cases.answer: I'd start from the output, not the prompt: define the exact fields we need - say issue_category, severity, customer_sentiment, requested_action - and their allowed values. Then I'd write the prompt backward from that schema, using structured output so parsing never breaks. I'd add 3-4 few-shot examples including the ugly cases: an empty ticket, an angry rant with no clear ask, a ticket mixing two issues. Before shipping I'd build a small labelled set, maybe 50 real tickets annotated by the support team, and set a bar like 90% field-level accuracy. Then I'd iterate on the failures specifically: bucket them, fix the biggest bucket (usually ambiguous category boundaries), re-run the set, and only ship when the bar holds. After shipping I'd keep sampling production outputs weekly to catch drift.
cases.note: Hits all four criteria: output-shape-first, few-shot + edge cases, concrete measurable bar, iterate-on-failures.

cases.answer: I would write a prompt that tells the model to summarize the ticket into the fields we want, then try it on a few tickets and see how it looks. If the output looks wrong I'd tweak the wording of the prompt and try again until the results look good. Once it seems to be working well on the tickets I tried, it's probably good enough to ship.
cases.note: Touches iteration but no output-shape thinking, no edge cases, no measurable bar - 'looks good' is eyeballing.

cases.answer: The key to reliable summarization is temperature tuning. I'd raise the temperature to around 1.2 so the model is more flexible and creative in understanding varied tickets, and I'd tell it in the prompt to be accurate. Higher temperature helps the model generalize to tickets it hasn't seen. Once it's creative enough to handle any ticket, it's ready to ship - accuracy comes from the model's intelligence, so testing isn't really the bottleneck.
cases.note: Fluent and on-vocabulary but factually backwards (high temperature hurts consistency) and rejects evaluation. Catches judges that reward fluency over substance.

cases.answer: For this feature I'd containerize the summarization service with Docker and deploy it behind a load balancer with autoscaling. I'd set up CI/CD so every change runs tests before deploy, add Prometheus metrics for latency and error rate, and use blue-green deployment so a bad release can be rolled back instantly. For reliability I'd add retries with exponential backoff on the LLM calls and a circuit breaker.
cases.note: Competent deployment answer that never addresses prompt design or iteration. Catches judges that reward general domain knowledge instead of the asked question.

cases.answer: Few-shot examples. Edge cases. Eval set. Target accuracy. Iterate on failures. Output schema. Constraints. Labelled data. Structured output. Ship when metrics pass.
cases.note: Bare rubric buzzwords with zero reasoning connecting them. Catches judges that pattern-match rubric words instead of judging understanding.

cases.answer: No, I wouldn't ship it as-is. The headline gain from 82% to 86% hides a serious regression: refunds dropped from 90% to 71%, a 19-point fall on what is likely a high-stakes category - refund mistakes cost money and anger customers. Billing and general improved, which is why the average looks good, but averages hide exactly this kind of damage. Next I'd pull the refunds failures from the eval set, diff them against the old prompt's outputs to see what the new version broke, fix that specifically, and re-run per-category metrics. I'd only ship once refunds is back near 90% while keeping the other gains - or ship gated so refund tickets keep using the old prompt meanwhile.
cases.note: Hits all expected insights: spots the hidden regression, says don't ship / ship gated, proposes drilling into refund failures, values per-segment over headline.

cases.answer: Looking at the data, overall accuracy went up from 82% to 86%, which is a 4-point improvement. Refunds went down from 90% to 71%, billing went up from 80% to 88%, and general went up from 79% to 85%. So two categories improved and one got worse. The overall number improved because the gains were bigger than the loss.
cases.note: Reads the numbers correctly but draws no conclusion - no ship/don't-ship decision, no next step. Description without judgment.

cases.answer: The data shows refunds improved from 71% to 90%, and since latency also dropped from 800ms to 300ms while cost fell 40%, this is a clear win across the board. With all categories above 95% accuracy now, I would ship immediately and announce the improvement to stakeholders.
cases.note: Cites numbers that are not in the dataset (latency, cost, 95%) and reverses the refunds direction. Verifies the judge checks claims against the provided data.

cases.answer: This is an interesting result that shows the complexity of evaluating LLM systems. The data reveals some patterns worth investigating further. I think more analysis is needed before making a final decision, and it would be good to gather more data and consult with the team about the best path forward.
cases.note: Says nothing falsifiable - no number read, no insight, no decision. Catches judges that reward polite hedging.

cases.answer: First I'd measure before touching anything: p50/p95 latency and cost per request, broken down by step, plus our eval-set score as the quality guardrail. Then the levers in rough order of impact: route easy cases to a smaller, cheaper model and keep the big model for hard ones; cache responses for repeated or near-duplicate inputs; cut prompt fat - shorter system prompt, trim retrieved context to what's actually used; stream tokens so perceived latency drops even where real latency can't. I'd change one lever at a time, re-run the eval set after each, and only keep changes where latency or cost improves with quality flat within a point or two. Prioritise by measured impact - if the model call is 90% of cost, prompt-trimming beats infrastructure work.
cases.note: Concrete levers, decisions tied to measured latency/cost, quality guarded by the eval set, prioritised by impact.
